Nucleophilic substitution. A fundamental class of organic reactions where an electron-rich nucleophile selectively bonds with or attacks an electron-deficient atom to displace a leaving group. This reaction class is central to functional group interconversions in organic synthesis, commonly occurring at saturated carbon centers.

The reaction proceeds via the SN2 pathway, a concerted bimolecular mechanism featuring back-side attack of the nucleophile, which results in Walden inversion of stereochemical configuration at the carbon center. Alternatively, it proceeds via the SN1 pathway, a stepwise unimolecular mechanism where the leaving group departs first to form a planar carbocation intermediate, leading to a racemic mixture of products.

The reaction is influenced by solvent polarity. Polar aprotic solvents, like DMSO and DMF, accelerate SN2 reactions by leaving nucleophiles unsolvated, while polar protic solvents like water promote SN1 by stabilizing carbocation intermediates. Steric hindrance governs the reaction mechanism, severely retarding SN2 reactions on secondary and tertiary carbons, rendering tertiary alkyl halides virtually inert to SN2 pathways. The reaction also correlates with leaving group stability, where weak bases—such as iodide, bromide, and tosylate—act as excellent leaving groups by stably accommodating negative charge.

Alkyl halides are the primary substrates for testing and performing aliphatic nucleophilic substitutions, and they also undergo a major competing reaction pathway called elimination, which occurs when a nucleophile also acts as a strong base. Hydroxide or water nucleophiles substitute halides to form alcohols, while alcohols can act as weak nucleophiles in solvolysis reactions.
